jurisdiction.name: Denver
jurisdiction.notes: City and County of Denver (consolidated, home-rule). Denver collects its own sales, lodger's and occupational privilege taxes through eBiz. The Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection (DLCP, formerly Excise & Licenses) issues business, food and liquor licenses. Community Planning & Development (CPD) runs zoning and building permits through E-permits. Denver's liquor entries cover both the city and state steps, because Denver approves locally first and won't issue the city license until the state license is issued. Plan for at least 120 days from a complete license application to issuance.

permits.name: Denver sales/use tax license (Treasury eBiz) – separate from the state license
permits.issuing_agency: City and County of Denver – Department of Finance, Treasury Division
permits.notes: Denver is a home-rule city, so you need a Denver tax account in addition to the Colorado sales tax license. There is no longer a license fee. Denver's rate is 4.00% on prepared food and drink (8.00% combined with state, RTD and district taxes) and 5.15% on general retail. Register and file in eBiz, or file sales/use tax through the state's SUTS portal using Denver code 01-0006. DLCP asks for the Denver sales tax license with retail food applications, and you need a Certificate of Taxes Due for liquor licensing.

permits.name: Denver Occupational Privilege Tax (OPT / 'head tax') employer registration
permits.issuing_agency: City and County of Denver – Department of Finance, Treasury Division
permits.notes: This is a Denver-only monthly tax. The business pays $4.00 per month for each employee earning $500+ in Denver in a month, plus $4.00 for each owner, partner or manager regardless of earnings. You also withhold $5.75 per month from each qualifying employee. Register in eBiz alongside your sales tax account and make sure your payroll provider is set up for Denver OPT before the first payroll.

permits.name: Denver Lodger's Tax registration (10.75%; 11.75% in the Tourism Improvement District)
permits.issuing_agency: City and County of Denver – Department of Finance, Treasury Division
permits.notes: Hotels and other paid accommodations collect Denver's 10.75% lodger's tax on stays under 30 days, or 14.75% combined with state, RTD and district taxes. Hotels with 50+ rooms also collect the Tourism Improvement District tax, for 11.75% Denver / 15.75% combined. It is added to the same eBiz account as sales tax, and the retailer's sales, use and lodger's tax license no longer carries a fee.

permits.name: Zoning use permit (eating & drinking establishment)
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Community Planning & Development (CPD) – Zoning
permits.notes: Every Denver business needs a zoning use permit for its use (e.g. 'eating & drinking establishment') at the address, and DLCP won't issue food or liquor licenses without it. Email CPD Records first to see if one already exists (allow 10 business days). You can apply for zoning alone or concurrently with the building log, and you can start license applications using an 'Acknowledgement of Zone Use Permit'. New construction or a change of occupancy with site impacts goes through a Site Development Plan, which issues the zoning permit.

permits.name: Commercial building permit ('building log') and Certificate of Occupancy
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Community Planning & Development (CPD) – Development Services
permits.notes: Submitting the 'building log' in E-permits starts building, DDPHE health, SUDP wastewater, fire and zoning reviews at the same time. Upload each discipline's documents up front. Plans must be sealed by licensed architects and engineers, and CPD advises one to two months of design work before applying. The CO isn't issued until every deferred submittal (often the walk-in cooler or patio) and every inspection is closed out. Check CPD's live review-times dashboard for current turnaround.
permits.stall_risk: Incomplete submittals and equipment swaps after permit issuance trigger modified-drawing reviews, which can stall the CO for weeks. Submit deferred items early and install exactly the equipment on the approved plans.

permits.name: DDPHE public health plan review and final sign-off inspection
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Department of Public Health and Environment (DDPHE) – Public Health Investigations
permits.notes: Full plan review is required for a change of use, new construction or an 'extensive remodel'. That includes a 20%+ seating increase, any alteration needing building-code review, a 25% change in back-of-house space, or a menu or process change that adds food-safety risk. Submit the Retail/Wholesale Food Establishment application and checklist items with the building log in E-permits. Before requesting the final TCO/CO sign-off, construction must be complete, equipment sealed in place, and hand sinks must deliver 85°F water within 30 seconds.

permits.name: Denver Retail Food Establishment license
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection (DLCP), with DDPHE inspection
permits.notes: Apply in Denver's online Permitting and Licensing Center with the zoning use permit, entity registration, on-site manager details and your Denver sales tax license. The fee is $150 to apply plus $25 for each food activity, such as cooking raw animal products, cooling, reheating or serving undercooked items. DLCP aims to review within seven business days and gives 14 days to cure deficiencies. Development Services, Denver Fire, DDPHE and Zoning then inspect before the license is emailed. Renew annually.

permits.name: Certified Food Protection Manager on staff (Denver)
permits.issuing_agency: ANSI-accredited exam provider (ServSafe, NRFSP, Prometric, etc.); enforced by DDPHE
permits.notes: Denver inspectors expect a Certified Food Protection Manager who passed an accredited exam to be on staff at food establishments that prepare food, even where other Colorado counties are looser. Certify the chef or GM before the DDPHE sign-off inspection. DDPHE also offers a free online Basic Food Safety Class (English and Spanish) for line staff.

permits.name: Hotel & Restaurant liquor license – Denver local + state (full liquor with meals)
permits.issuing_agency: Denver DLCP (local licensing authority) + Colorado Liquor Enforcement Division
permits.notes: You file one packet with DLCP: the city application ($1,000 plus assigned fees) and the state application ($1,100, or $1,200 for concurrent review) plus license fees. Include evidence of neighborhood 'need and desire' (petitions from the designated area, witness affidavits, RNO/BID letters, Good Neighbor Agreements). After review you post notice, the Director may set a public hearing, and fingerprints take 10–15 days. Inspections start after hearing approval, and the city license issues only after the state license. Requires a full kitchen, meals 8 a.m.–8 p.m., and 25%+ of income from food. Service runs 7 a.m.–2 a.m.
permits.stall_risk: Weak need-and-desire evidence or an objecting Registered Neighborhood Organization leads to a discretionary public hearing. Neighbors often demand a Good Neighbor Agreement (patio hours, noise, trash) as the price of support. Meet the RNOs and collect petitions before filing, since evidence submitted with the application speeds processing.

permits.name: Tavern liquor license – Denver local + state (full-liquor bar)
permits.issuing_agency: Denver DLCP (local licensing authority) + Colorado Liquor Enforcement Division
permits.notes: This license is for bars serving beer, wine and spirits with at least sandwiches and light snacks available. It uses the same dual city + state packet, need-and-desire evidence, posting and possible hearing as Hotel & Restaurant. Unlike H&R in Denver, a 500-ft distance restriction from schools, colleges and seminaries applies. Every tavern manager must register with the city and state ($30 each, fingerprints), and a manager may run only one tavern. Hours are 7 a.m.–2 a.m.
permits.stall_risk: Bars draw far more neighborhood opposition than restaurants, especially in RiNo, LoHi and Capitol Hill. Expect a hearing and Good Neighbor Agreement negotiations, and confirm the school distance before signing a lease.

permits.name: Beer & Wine liquor license – Denver local + state
permits.issuing_agency: Denver DLCP (local licensing authority) + Colorado Liquor Enforcement Division
permits.notes: This license covers beer and wine by the drink for cafes, wine bars and casual restaurants. It goes through the same Denver process (zoning use permit, need-and-desire evidence, posting, possible hearing, inspections, state approval before city issuance) at slightly lower state license fees. A brewery taproom or brewpub uses the Brew Pub license instead.

permits.name: Lodging Facility liquor license – Denver local + state (hotels)
permits.issuing_agency: Denver DLCP (local licensing authority) + Colorado Liquor Enforcement Division
permits.notes: This is the hotel-wide liquor license that replaced the old Lodging & Entertainment class. Hotels whose main restaurant meets the meal and 25% food-revenue rules often hold a Hotel & Restaurant license with optional premises instead. Same Denver dual city/state process and timeline as other liquor licenses.

permits.name: Cabaret license (live entertainment, DJs, dancing) – becoming Entertainment Business licenses April 2027
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection (DLCP)
permits.notes: Denver still requires a cabaret license, added to an existing liquor license, for live entertainment including DJs and karaoke, or patron dancing. Standard and acoustic licenses cost $500 to apply plus $750, and dance or special-dance licenses $1,000 plus $1,500. Letting in patrons aged 16+ needs an underage endorsement ($200 + $750). Council Bill 26-0921 (signed Aug 5, 2026) replaces cabaret licenses with Limited, Nightlife and Adult Entertainment Business licenses effective April 1, 2027, with new security-plan and hearing rules. Venues opening near that date should plan for the new license.
permits.stall_risk: Cabaret applications follow the liquor license and invite noise complaints from neighbors and RNOs. Dance cabarets in mixed-use areas often face hearings or conditions. Under the 2027 code, nightlife licenses will also need security and video-surveillance plans, so budget for those.

permits.name: Denver Fire Department plan review, hood suppression and occupancy inspection
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Fire Department – Fire Prevention Division
permits.notes: DFD reviews egress, occupant load, alarms and sprinklers as part of the building log. Kitchen hood extinguishing systems qualify for a walk-through review about two business days after acceptance. The initial occupancy and life-safety system inspections are free, but failed reinspections cost $500, then $800 each. Request inspections in Accela Citizen Access. One-off events in assembly spaces need a DFD Special Event permit at least 45 days ahead.

permits.name: Sign zoning permit (plus right-of-way permit for projecting signs)
permits.issuing_agency: Denver CPD – Zoning; DOTI Right-of-Way Services for signs over the public way
permits.notes: Most permanent signs on private property need a zoning sign permit, and blade or projecting signs over the sidewalk also need a DOTI right-of-way permit. Illuminated signs need an electrical permit. Signs in historic districts (much of LoDo and parts of Capitol Hill) need Landmark design approval first. Unlit temporary window signs for up to 45 days are exempt.

permits.name: Sewer Use & Drainage Permit (SUDP) – grease interceptor / FOG pretreatment review
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Department of Transportation & Infrastructure (DOTI) – Wastewater / SUDP
permits.notes: The SUDP team reviews every food-service project in the building log for grease and solids interceptors. They check the menu, kitchen equipment, plumbing and site utility plans. Under Denver's new grease interceptor policy, every kitchen, prep and warewashing sink, hand sinks included, must drain through the interceptor, while bar-only beverage sinks must not. A change of owner alone usually keeps the existing interceptor, but menu, seating or equipment changes trigger review.
permits.stall_risk: If the existing interceptor is undersized or missing, you may need a new exterior interceptor with site-utility design, excavation and DOTI approval, which can add months and five figures. Have a plumbing engineer size it against the menu before signing the lease.

permits.name: Outdoor Places / right-of-way patio encroachment permit (sidewalk or parking-lane patio)
permits.issuing_agency: Denver DOTI – Right-of-Way Services, Land Use and Permanent Occupancy (LUPO)
permits.notes: Since the 2026 Outdoor Places update, right-of-way patios are issued as Tier I/II/III Encroachment Permits by DOTI LUPO, which offers a free tier determination. Above-curb sidewalk patios get lighter review than below-curb patios in parking lanes. A Street Occupancy request is also needed. The permit doesn't expire, but owners get a $200 annual invoice. Patios on your own lot are approved instead through a commercial zoning permit (Outdoor Gathering Area, DZC 11.10.14).
permits.stall_risk: Serving alcohol on the patio needs a permanent Modification of Premises from DLCP and the state on top of the encroachment permit. That adds weeks, so file both together and keep the patio off the liquor premises diagram until it is approved.

permits.name: Denver Lodging Facility business license (4+ rooms)
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection (DLCP)
permits.notes: Any hotel, lodging house or other place renting four or more rooms to transients needs this license. Fees scale with rooms: $100 application plus $100 license for 4–25 units, up to $300 plus $200 for over 200. DLCP aims to review within seven business days, and required inspections follow before the license is emailed. Separate from the liquor Lodging Facility license and from lodger's tax registration.

permits.name: Retail Food Mobile license (food truck / cart)
permits.issuing_agency: Denver DLCP, with DDPHE packet review and Denver Fire inspection
permits.notes: The truck must be fully built before applying. Submit the mobile plan review packet (or a state mobile license under reciprocity), a commissary affidavit, equipment spec sheets and photos. The fee is $150 plus $25 per food activity. DDPHE reviews the packet remotely within 7–10 business days and DFD inspects in person, after which DLCP emails the license within five business days. Parking is restricted in parts of downtown, and a zoning use permit is needed when operating on private property.

permits.name: Denver Fire propane operational permit and mobile food vending fire inspection
permits.issuing_agency: Denver Fire Department – Fire Prevention Division
permits.notes: Trucks using propane apply online for a Fire Prevention Flammable Operational Permit (an annual $200 fee, invoiced in 5–7 business days) with registration, driver's license and a current suppression-system report. DFD's 2026 fee schedule also lists a $250 annual Mobile Food Vending permit. Every new truck must pass a DFD safety inspection (dfdmobiles@denvergov.org), though a current FMAC Certificate of Inspection from another Colorado agency is accepted. Don't apply until the unit is ready to inspect.
